n: David calls urgently: ‘Lord, hurry to me; listen when I call.’
May his prayer rise to God like the fragrant incense in the temple, and his raised hands be like the evening offering. Prayer itself is a form of sacrifice.
He asks God to station a guard at his mouth and watch the door of his lips. Controlling speech is a spiritual discipline.

f.w: Set a watch, O LORD, before my mouth

n: ‘Don’t let my heart lean toward evil, or let me join evildoers or enjoy their delicacies.’ The perks of wicked company are a temptation too.
He welcomes correction from the righteous as a kindness — like soothing oil on the head rather than a blow. Even so, he keeps praying against the wicked’s deeds.

f.w: Let the righteous smite me; it shall be a kindness

f.g: Fine oil for anointing the head — refreshing and honoring.

n: A difficult verse. When the wicked leaders are thrown down from the cliffs, people will finally listen and find David’s words pleasant and true.

f.g: Down the sides of a rocky cliff.

n: Another obscure line: their (or our) bones lie scattered at the mouth of the grave like chips of wood or clods turned up by a plow.

f.g: The entrance to Sheol, the realm of the dead.

n: But David keeps his eyes on God, trusting him. ‘Don’t leave my life defenseless’ — literally, ‘don’t pour out my soul.’

f.g: Don’t pour out my life; don’t leave me exposed.

n: Keep me from the traps and snares the wicked have set.
Let the wicked fall into their own nets while David passes by safely.

f.w: Let the wicked fall into their own nets
